what_it_does: Memory disaggregation is the idea of placing memory chips in a separate box from the processor and accessing them over a network cable (Ethernet), so that large pools of memory can be shared or expanded without redesigning the whole server. The catch is that standard networking protocols — TCP/IP (the rules your browser uses) and RDMA/RoCEv2 (a faster variant used in data centers) — all run on top of a hardware layer called the MAC layer (think of it as the traffic cop that manages each cable's turns), and that traffic-cop overhead adds hundreds of nanoseconds of delay even before any real data moves. EDM bypasses the MAC layer entirely by implementing its memory-access protocol inside the physical signaling layer (PHY) of Ethernet — the layer that directly controls the electrical or optical signals on the wire. A smart switch running inside that same physical layer acts as a central matchmaker, reserving dedicated, collisionless paths between compute nodes and memory nodes on the fly. A prototype built on FPGA hardware (a type of reconfigurable chip used for rapid prototyping) achieved roughly 300 nanoseconds of round-trip delay for a remote memory read — far lower than existing approaches.
